newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak FinMin sees 97 trade deficit static -paper.
newsitem.headline: Slovak FinMin sees 97 trade deficit static -paper.

text.p: Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik said the country's trade deficit should not exceed that of 1996, and total around 60 billion crowns, the economic weekly Trend reported on Thursday.

"I think that this year we should not exceed the 1996 figure (of the trade deficit), and that this should then amount to around 60 billion crowns," Kozlik said in an interview in the weekly's latest edition.
Slovakia posted a 1996 trade deficit of 64.54 billion crowns, up from a 5.69 billion crown shortfall in 1995.
Kozlik said the widening trade deficit represented a significant risk for macroeconomic stability but that the structure of the deficit was not too dangerous.
The trade deficit more than trebled in January 1997 year-on-year, totalling 7.06 billion crowns, compared with a 2.13 billion crown shortfall in January 1996.
Kozlik said imports were boosted mainly by purchases of raw materials, such as iron ore, crude oil and gas, and that imports of nuclear materials and technology were also increasing.

"These purchases (nuclear materials and technology) will play a significant role in the trade balance until the completion and launch of the first part of the Mochovce nuclear power plant," Kozlik said.

"Once the first Mochovce block is operational, exports of electricity should compensate for the imports neccessary to complete the second block" he added. The first block of Mochovce is scheduled to be completed in 1998.
The government will not re-introduce an unpopular import surcharge, scrapped at the beginning of this year, to slowdown the widening trade balance, Kozlik said.

Government officials, including Kozlik, have said the negative trend of the trade balance should be curbed by an active export policy, using the newly-created Export-Import bank or the State Fund to Support Exports, rather than imposing administrative protectionist measures.
But Kozlik said one of the tools to curb the trade deficit would be a law on protection against excessive imports, now being drafted, and the already-approved law banning imports at dumping prices.
